PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY__X-ray Head & N:
The plain skull X-ray is a piece of imaging history that still lingers in exams. Its role in modern practice is very limited: for head injury, CT head — not a skull film — is the investigation that detects intracranial injury. Learn the handful of niche indications that remain, and the metabolic/bone patterns beloved of examiners.

1Why it has fallen out of favour

A skull fracture on plain film neither confirms nor excludes brain injury, and finding one rarely changes management. NICE head injury guidance triages patients to CT head to detect intracranial haemorrhage and other injury — the skull X-ray is not used to make that decision. A normal skull film must never reassure you in a patient with a significant head injury.

Significant head injury→CT head, not skull X-ray
2Standard views

When a skull series is taken, it typically includes:

PA / AP — frontal projection of the vault, orbits and facial bones.
Lateral — profiles the vault, sella turcica (pituitary fossa), sinuses and calcification.
Towne's view — angled AP projecting the occiput free of overlying bone, for occipital fractures.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph.
3A systematic look

Assess the vault for fracture lines, the sutures, the sella turcica, the sinuses and any calcification. The key trap is telling a fracture from its mimics: a fracture is a lucent line that is sharp, non-branching and does not follow a known suture or vascular groove. Vascular markings branch and taper; sutures run in fixed anatomical positions with a serrated edge.

Lucent line, sharp, straight, non-branching, crosses sutures/vessels→Fracture
4The indications that remain

A short list of situations where a skull X-ray still earns its place:

🧩Suspected NAI
Skull forms part of the paediatric skeletal survey in suspected non-accidental injury, searching for occult fractures.
🔩Foreign body
Localising a radio-opaque foreign body (e.g. metal, glass) in or around the head.
🦴Metabolic / bone disease
Classic patterns: myeloma, hyperparathyroidism, Paget's, thalassaemia (see below).
🧠Sella / shunt series
An enlarged sella turcica hinted a pituitary tumour (now MRI); a shunt series checks VP shunt continuity.
5Exam-favourite bone patterns
Multiple myeloma — multiple well-defined lytic "punched-out" lesions.
Hyperparathyroidism — "pepperpot" / salt-and-pepper granular skull from subperiosteal resorption.
Paget's disease — "cotton wool" patches of sclerosis; osteoporosis circumscripta as a lytic phase; thickened vault.
Thalassaemia — "hair-on-end" vertical trabeculae from marrow expansion.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph.
🚩 A significant head injury needs a CT head, never a skull X-ray — a normal skull film does not exclude intracranial injury. In suspected non-accidental injury, do not stop at imaging: make an urgent safeguarding referral and arrange a full skeletal survey.
🎓 If a question offers you a skull X-ray for an adult head injury, it is almost always the wrong answer — reach for CT head. The skull film survives mainly as a pattern-recognition tool (punched-out myeloma, pepperpot hyperparathyroidism, cotton-wool Paget's, hair-on-end thalassaemia) and as part of the paediatric skeletal survey.

The facial bones X-ray is the traditional first-line imaging for suspected facial trauma, though CT has now become the definitive investigation for complex mid-face and orbital injuries. Your job on a plain film is to interrogate the facial skeleton systematically, spot subtle fractures and their tell-tale secondary signs, and recognise when a patient needs urgent maxillofacial referral or a CT.

1Get the standard views right

The workhorses are the occipitomental (OM / "Waters") views taken at 15° and 30°. These project the petrous temporal bones below the maxillary antra, giving you a clear look at the facial skeleton, orbits, maxillary sinuses and zygomatic arches. The two angulations help distinguish overlapping structures and confirm whether a suspicious line is a genuine fracture on both projections.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph: OM (Waters) view showing the orbits, maxillary antra and zygomatic arches, with the petrous ridges projected clear of the sinuses.
2Trace McGrigor–Campbell lines

Bring order to the film with three horizontal McGrigor–Campbell lines, following each across from one side to the other and comparing left with right — asymmetry is the clue to a fracture.

Line 1→across the zygomatico-frontal sutures and superior orbital margins
Line 2→across the zygomatic arches, inferior orbital margins and roofs of the maxillary antra
Line 3→across the mandibular condyles and the occlusal line
Follow each line as a smooth continuous curve; a step, break or discontinuity where the line crosses bone is a fracture until proven otherwise.
3Recognise the key fractures

Certain patterns recur and each has classic radiographic features:

🦴Zygomatic complex
The "tripod"/quadripod fracture: disruption at the zygomatico-frontal suture, inferior orbital rim and zygomatic arch. Look for a step in the orbital rim and antral opacification.
💧Orbital blowout
Fracture of the orbital floor with herniation of orbital contents into the maxillary sinus — the "teardrop" sign hanging into the antral roof, with opacification or a fluid level.
👃Nasoethmoidal
Fractures of the nasal bones and ethmoid complex, often with telecanthus and epistaxis; a CT is needed to define the injury.
🔨Le Fort I / II / III
Mid-face fractures of increasing severity, from the low transverse maxilla (I) through the pyramidal (II) to complete craniofacial disjunction (III). Suspect on any mobile mid-face.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph: OM view of a left orbital blowout with a soft-tissue "teardrop" projecting from the orbital floor into the maxillary antrum and a fluid level in the sinus.
4Read the secondary signs

The fracture line itself may be invisible; the injury often announces itself through indirect signs. A fluid level in a maxillary sinus after trauma represents blood (a haemoantrum) and strongly implies a fracture. Soft-tissue emphysema — lucent streaks of air in the soft tissues — signals communication with an air-containing sinus. Clinically, orbital floor fractures cause enophthalmos and diplopia with restricted upgaze from tethering of the inferior rectus.

Fluid level in the maxillary antrum after trauma→haemoantrum — assume an underlying facial fracture
🚩 An orbital blowout fracture with entrapment — restricted eye movements, diplopia on upgaze and a non-axial (sunken or displaced) globe — is a surgical concern requiring urgent maxillofacial and ophthalmology referral. Never forget the associated dangers: a suspected complex mid-face, Le Fort or orbital injury needs a CT facial bones; always look for associated head and c-spine injury; and retrobulbar haemorrhage (a tense, proptosed, painful eye with falling acuity) is a sight-threatening emergency needing immediate decompression.
🎓 On any facial trauma film, discipline beats intuition: run the three McGrigor–Campbell lines, compare left with right, and treat a fluid level in the maxillary sinus as a fracture until proven otherwise. But remember the plain film's limits — if the mid-face is mobile, the globe is displaced or the injury looks complex, the answer is a CT and a phone call, not another X-ray view.

A nasal X-ray is one of the most requested and least useful radiographs in the emergency department. A simple, isolated nasal fracture is a clinical diagnosis — the film does not change what you do. NICE and ENT practice is clear: do not routinely image a suspected isolated nasal fracture. Your job at the bedside is to look for the things that actually matter: a septal haematoma, a functional or cosmetic deformity, and any sign of a more serious injury such as CSF rhinorrhoea.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph. Lateral nasal bones view showing the nasal bone with a lucent fracture line; note how the normal nasofrontal suture and nasociliary groove can mimic a fracture and mislead the unwary.
1Why the X-ray is (almost) never indicated

The plain nasal X-ray is unreliable — normal sutures and vascular grooves mimic fractures, and genuine fractures are often invisible. Crucially, it does not change management: the decision to manipulate depends on the clinical deformity, not the film. So you assess and manage clinically.

Isolated nasal injury, no other concern → No X-ray — examine, document, plan clinical review
If imaging is ever performed, the views are the lateral nasal and the occipitomental (OM) — but this is the exception, not the routine.
2The must-not-miss: septal haematoma

Every patient with nasal trauma must have the inside of the nose examined. A septal haematoma is a boggy, often bilateral swelling on the nasal septum. If missed, pressure and infection cause septal cartilage necrosis and abscess, leading to a collapsed saddle-nose deformity.

Boggy septal swelling on speculum exam → Urgent incision & drainage — do not wait
3Deformity and the manipulation window

Early swelling hides the true shape of the nose, so review the patient at 5–7 days once it settles to judge deformity. If manipulation (MUA) is needed, it is best done within about 10–14 days (2 weeks) of injury — after that the bones begin to set and a later formal rhinoplasty may be required.

Persistent deformity at review → MUA within ~2 weeks of injury, before bones fix
📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph. CT of the facial bones (not a nasal X-ray) demonstrating an anterior skull base / cribriform plate fracture — the appropriate imaging when CSF rhinorrhoea is suspected.
4Exclude a more serious injury

Look beyond the nose. Clear fluid rhinorrhoea after trauma suggests a cribriform plate / anterior skull base fracture with a CSF leak. This needs a CT head/facial bones and neurosurgical input — never a nasal X-ray. Also actively screen for other facial fractures (orbit, zygoma, midface).

💧CSF rhinorrhoea
Clear fluid, halo/tramline sign, beta-2-transferrin positive → CT + neurosurgery.
🩸Septal haematoma
Boggy septal swelling → urgent drainage to prevent saddle-nose.
🚩 A septal haematoma is the must-not-miss bedside finding — always examine inside the nose and drain it urgently. Separately, CSF rhinorrhoea (clear fluid, positive halo/tramline sign, confirmed by beta-2-transferrin) signals a skull base fracture needing CT and neurosurgery — this is never a job for a nasal X-ray.
🎓 If a student ever "orders a nasal X-ray" in a station, they have already gone wrong. Simple nasal fracture = clinical diagnosis; the film changes nothing. Examine the septum, arrange a 5–7 day review, manipulate within ~2 weeks if deformed, and escalate a suspected CSF leak to CT — not to radiography of the nasal bones.

The orthopantomogram (OPG) — also called the DPT (dental panoramic tomogram) — is a single curved-plane tomographic image that unrolls the whole mandible, maxilla, all teeth and both TMJs onto one film. In the ED it is the workhorse for suspected mandibular trauma; in dentistry it screens caries, periapical disease and impacted third molars.

1What the OPG shows & why we order it

One panoramic sweep captures the entire dental arch and jaws. Common indications:

🦴Mandibular fracture
Trauma, malocclusion — the number-one ED indication.
🦷Dental pathology
Caries, periapical abscess, impacted / wisdom teeth.
🔵Cysts & tumours
Jaw cysts, ameloblastoma, osteomyelitis.
⚙️TMJ & pre-extraction
TMJ assessment; planning before tooth extraction.
📷 Image placeholder — normal OPG: panoramic view of both condyles, rami, angles, bodies and symphysis with a full dentition and both TMJs.
2The ring principle — always look for a SECOND fracture

The mandible is a bony ring (think of a polo mint). Snap a rigid ring in one place and the force usually breaks it in a second place too, so mandibular fractures are frequently bilateral.

Fracture of the body / parasymphysis on one side→Hunt hard for a contralateral condylar or angle fracture — the classic exam pairing.
Lucent line crossing the cortex.
A step or break in the lower-border cortex.
Clinical malocclusion / abnormal bite.
A tooth sitting in the fracture line.
3Reading the OPG systematically — walk the ring

Trace the whole ring in order so no segment is missed; the OPG can foreshorten the condyles, so pair it with a PA mandible or reverse-Towne's view.

Condyles — symmetry, position within the fossa.
Rami — vertical struts, cortical continuity.
Angles — common site, often near the third molar.
Body — lower-border cortex for a step.
Symphysis / parasymphysis — anterior midline.
Alveolar margin & teeth — count teeth, note any in a fracture line.
📷 Image placeholder — OPG showing a right parasymphyseal fracture with a lucent step in the lower border AND a subtle contralateral left condylar neck fracture (the missed second fracture).
🚩 A bilateral anterior / parasymphyseal ("bucket-handle") fracture can let the anterior fragment and tongue fall backwards and obstruct the airway — a true emergency (sit the patient forward, pull the tongue/fragment forward, secure the airway). Any fracture through the tooth-bearing segment is effectively an open (compound) fracture — give antibiotics and make an urgent maxillofacial referral. And never forget: look for the second fracture.
🎓 The mandible is a ring — one fracture invites another, so a single obvious fracture on the OPG should trigger a deliberate hunt around the whole ring for its contralateral partner (classically body/parasymphysis with a condylar or angle fracture).

The lateral soft tissue neck X-ray is a plain radiograph coned to the airway column and prevertebral tissues. It answers a small number of specific questions — is there a radio-opaque foreign body lodged in the pharynx or upper oesophagus, is the upper airway of a sick child obstructed by infection, and are the prevertebral soft tissues abnormally swollen. It is never the priority when the airway itself is threatened.

1Know why it was ordered
Three classic indications. First, a suspected radio-opaque foreign body — an impacted fish or chicken bone in the tonsil, vallecula, pyriform fossa or upper oesophagus (remember many fish bones are radiolucent, so a normal film does not exclude one). Second, a child with suspected upper airway infection where you are weighing croup against epiglottitis against retropharyngeal abscess. Third, assessment of the prevertebral soft tissues after trauma or for suspected deep neck space infection. It also demonstrates surgical emphysema.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph. Normal lateral soft tissue neck: thin, uniform prevertebral stripe anterior to the cervical vertebral bodies, a clearly aerated airway column, a well-defined thin epiglottis and normal vallecular air.
2Get the technique right
The film should be taken in inspiration with the neck extended. This is the single biggest source of misinterpretation: a film taken in flexion or expiration falsely widens the prevertebral soft tissues and can mimic a retropharyngeal collection. Before you call swelling, confirm the child is not simply flexed or breathing out.
Poorly aerated, flexed, expiratory film→apparent prevertebral widening that disappears on a proper inspiratory extended film — repeat before over-calling
3Recognise the killer patterns
Match the clinical picture to the film. The three infective causes each have a signature — but epiglottitis is a signature you should rarely be chasing on film, because it is a clinical airway emergency.
👍Epiglottitis — Thumbprint sign
Swollen, rounded epiglottis on the lateral film resembling a thumbprint, often with thickened aryepiglottic folds. Typically the older, toxic, drooling child sitting forward. A clinical emergency — do not force imaging.
⛪Croup — Steeple sign
Subglottic narrowing from laryngotracheobronchitis producing a tapered steeple shape — but this is a frontal (AP/PA) sign, not a lateral one. Barking cough, stridor, usually a well-appearing younger child.
📏Retropharyngeal abscess — Prevertebral widening
Prevertebral soft tissue wider than the adjacent vertebral body, sometimes with gas or an air-fluid level. The child holds the neck extended and resists movement. Needs urgent ENT referral.
Prevertebral soft tissue rule of thumb: greater than about 7 mm at C2, and greater than about 14–22 mm at C6. Above C6 the tissues are normally thin; below C6 they thicken where the oesophagus begins, so use the correct level for the correct threshold.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph. Retropharyngeal abscess: markedly widened prevertebral stripe far exceeding the width of the vertebral body, bowing the airway anteriorly, with a possible lucency or air-fluid level within the swelling.
🚩 Suspected epiglottitis is an airway emergency. Do NOT lie the child down, do NOT examine the throat or depress the tongue, and do NOT send them for an X-ray that could precipitate complete obstruction. Keep the child calm and upright with a parent, and get senior anaesthetic and ENT help to secure the airway first. A retropharyngeal abscess or an impacted sharp foreign body also warrants urgent ENT referral.
🎓 The lateral soft tissue neck film is a supporting actor, not the lead. When the airway is stable it can confirm a radio-opaque bone, prevertebral widening or surgical emphysema — but the moment epiglottitis is on your list, the film comes after a secured airway, never before it. Always sanity-check technique (inspiration, extension) before calling prevertebral swelling.
PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY__X-ray Spine:
The cervical spine radiograph is a classic exam and on-call scenario, but the single most important modern point is knowing when NOT to use it. In significant trauma, plain films miss injuries, and current NICE practice favours CT cervical spine. Clinical decision rules — the Canadian C-Spine Rule and NEXUS — decide who needs imaging at all. When plain films are used, they must be read systematically and must be adequate.

1Decide who needs imaging — the decision rules

Not every neck-pain patient needs a film. Two validated rules screen out low-risk patients:

NEXUS — imaging can be avoided if ALL five are met: no midline cervical tenderness, no focal neurological deficit, normal alertness, no intoxication, no distracting injury.

Canadian C-Spine Rule — considers high-risk factors (age ≥65, dangerous mechanism, paraesthesiae in limbs), low-risk factors that permit safe assessment of movement (e.g. simple rear-end collision, sitting/ambulatory, delayed onset pain, no midline tenderness), and whether the patient can actively rotate the neck 45° each way.

Significant trauma or rule failed→CT cervical spine (not plain film) is the modern investigation of choice
2The three views

If plain films are used, a standard series is three views:

Lateral — most informative view. Must visualise from C1 down to the C7/T1 junction. A common and dangerous failure is not seeing down to T1 (obscured by shoulders) — the film is then inadequate and cannot clear the c-spine.
AP — assesses vertical alignment of spinous processes and lateral masses.
Peg / open-mouth (odontoid) view — shows the odontoid peg (dens) and the C1 lateral masses relative to C2, to detect dens fractures and lateral mass asymmetry (Jefferson).
📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph: lateral cervical spine showing C1 through the C7/T1 junction, with the four alignment lines to be traced.
3Systematic reading — "ABCS" on the lateral

Read every lateral in the same order so nothing is missed:

A — Adequacy: is C7/T1 seen? If not, the film cannot clear the c-spine (consider swimmer's view or CT).
A — Alignment: trace FOUR smooth curved lines — (1) anterior vertebral body line, (2) posterior vertebral body line, (3) spinolaminar line, (4) tips of the spinous processes. Any step or break suggests malalignment. Also note loss of the normal cervical lordosis.
B — Bone: follow the cortex of each vertebra; look for lucent fracture lines, cortical breaks, and vertebral body height loss.
C — Cartilage: assess the disc/intervertebral spaces and interspinous distances — widening of an interspinous gap suggests ligamentous injury.
S — Soft tissues: prevertebral soft tissue widening indicates blood/oedema and is a clue to occult fracture (roughly <7 mm at C2, and up to the width of a vertebral body at C6/C7).
📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph: annotated lateral showing widened prevertebral soft tissue shadow anterior to C2–C3 in a patient with an odontoid fracture.
4Key injuries to recognise
🦴Odontoid (dens) fracture
Fracture of the C2 peg; best seen on peg view/lateral. Common in elderly falls; can be unstable.
💥Jefferson (C1 burst)
Axial-load burst of the C1 ring; peg view shows lateral masses splayed outward beyond C2.
🪢Hangman's (C2)
Bilateral C2 pars/pedicle fracture from hyperextension; often with anterolisthesis of C2 on C3.
💧Flexion teardrop
Triangular fragment off the antero-inferior vertebral body; severe unstable flexion injury, high cord-injury risk.
🔓Facet dislocation
Uni-/bilateral "jumped" facets; look for a step in alignment lines and widened interspinous distance.
⛏️Clay-shoveler's (C7)
Avulsion of a lower cervical (classically C7) spinous process; typically stable but must not be mistaken.
🚩 Any suspected unstable cervical spine injury — keep the neck fully immobilised (hard collar plus blocks/tape) and do not remove it. If the mechanism, symptoms or films are concerning, obtain CT cervical spine (± MRI for cord or ligamentous injury). High cervical injuries risk respiratory compromise — watch the airway and breathing. NEVER clear a c-spine on an inadequate lateral that does not show down to C7/T1.

🎓 The four alignment lines should each form a single smooth curve — a step of even a couple of millimetres in any one of them, loss of the normal lordosis, a widened interspinous gap, or prevertebral soft-tissue swelling are all red flags for injury, and when in doubt the safe move is immobilise and CT rather than trusting a normal-looking plain film.

The thoracic spine X-ray (AP and lateral) is a first-line plain film for back pain with red flags, trauma, suspected vertebral compression fracture (osteoporotic or pathological), deformity (kyphosis/scoliosis) and screening for metastatic disease. It is cheap and quick but insensitive early on — in high-energy trauma CT is preferred, and cord compression is a job for MRI, not a plain film.

📷 Image placeholder — AP thoracic spine: describe the vertical column of vertebral bodies, the paired oval pedicles either side of each body (the "owl's eyes"), and the paraspinal soft-tissue lines.
1Review systematically — ABCs adapted for the spine

Alignment: follow the anterior and posterior vertebral body lines and the spinous processes — should form smooth unbroken curves. Vertebral body height and endplates: compare the anterior and posterior height of each body; look for cortical breaks or step-offs at the superior/inferior endplates. Each vertebra and disc space: work down level by level, checking disc spaces are preserved and roughly equal. Pedicles (AP view): each vertebra should show two symmetric oval pedicle shadows.

Smooth alignment, uniform body height, intact endplates, paired symmetric pedicles = normal.
2Osteoporotic wedge / compression fracture

Anterior wedging with loss of anterior vertebral body height, most often in the mid-to-lower thoracic spine of an elderly (often osteoporotic) patient. Frequently multiple levels, and cumulative anterior wedging produces an exaggerated thoracic kyphosis. Endplate cortex is usually preserved and the pedicles are intact — features that favour a benign osteoporotic cause.

Elderly patient, sudden back pain after minimal trauma→anterior wedge fracture, think osteoporosis
📷 Image placeholder — Lateral thoracic spine: describe an anteriorly wedged vertebral body with reduced anterior height and resulting kyphotic angulation.
3Pathological fracture & metastasis — the winking owl

On the AP view the two pedicles look like an owl's eyes. Tumour destruction of one pedicle makes it disappear — the "winking owl" / absent pedicle" sign, a classic clue to metastatic bone destruction. Other pointers: vertebral body destruction, a fracture at an unusual level, posterior cortex involvement, and diffuse vertebral collapse (think myeloma). Check the paraspinal lines — widening suggests a soft-tissue mass or haematoma.

One pedicle missing on the AP film→winking owl = metastatic destruction until proven otherwise

Classic bone-metastasising primaries — remember Prostate, Breast, Lung, Kidney, Thyroid.

🦴Osteoporotic wedge fracture
Anterior wedging, preserved endplate cortex & pedicles, often multiple → kyphosis; elderly.
🦉Metastatic / pathological fracture
Absent pedicle (winking owl), body destruction, fracture at odd level; PBLKT primaries.
🩸Multiple myeloma collapse
Diffuse vertebral collapse / lytic lesions; consider in unexplained multilevel loss of height.
📏Widened paraspinal line
Soft-tissue mass or post-traumatic haematoma alongside the thoracic spine.
🚩 Back pain with RED FLAGS — thoracic pain, age <20 or >55, night pain, weight loss, history of cancer, neurological signs, saddle anaesthesia, or bladder/bowel dysfunction — must not be reassured on the basis of a normal plain film. Suspect malignancy / metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC) or infection. MSCC needs urgent whole-spine MRI, dexamethasone, and immediate oncology/spinal referral; a pathological or unstable fracture also needs urgent referral.
🎓 The thoracic X-ray raises the suspicion, MRI makes the diagnosis. A normal film never excludes cord compression — if the red flags are there, escalate to whole-spine MRI regardless of what the plain film shows.

The lumbosacral spine radiograph (AP and lateral) is one of the most over-requested plain films in medicine — and one of the least useful. For non-specific low back pain, NICE advises against routine lumbar X-rays: they deliver a substantial gonadal radiation dose (a lumbar spine series is many times the dose of a chest film) and almost never change management. Know the handful of legitimate indications, the few findings you can actually read off plain film, and — above all — the red flags that mean the patient needs an urgent MRI, not an X-ray.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph. Normal AP and lateral lumbosacral spine: five lumbar vertebrae with preserved disc spaces, aligned anterior and posterior vertebral body lines, and intact pedicles giving the AP "owl's eyes" appearance.
1When is a plain film actually justified?

The key message: routine imaging is not indicated for non-specific low back pain. Reserve plain radiographs for specific questions they can answer.

Significant trauma, or query spondylolisthesis / spondylolysis, inflammatory back pain screen, scoliosis / deformity, or checking metalwork→plain film is reasonable
Suspected radiculopathy, cauda equina, infection or malignancy→go straight to MRI — X-ray adds nothing

MRI is the investigation of choice for suspected serious pathology because it shows the cord, cauda equina, discs, marrow and soft tissue that plain film cannot.

2A system for reading the film

Use alignment, bones, cartilage (disc) spaces and soft tissues — then look specifically at the pars and the sacroiliac joints.

Alignment — trace the smooth anterior and posterior vertebral body lines on the lateral. A step-off suggests slip (spondylolisthesis) or fracture.
Disc spaces — narrowing indicates degenerative disc disease; loss with endplate erosion raises discitis / osteomyelitis (needs MRI).
Bones — osteophytes, endplate sclerosis, facet arthropathy (degenerative); lytic or sclerotic lesions and loss of a pedicle ("winking owl" sign) raise malignancy.
Pars interarticularis — best seen on oblique views; a defect breaks the "Scottie dog" neck.
Sacroiliac joints & count — assess for sacroiliitis; count segments to spot a transitional vertebra.
3Key structural findings
🦴Degenerative change
Disc space narrowing, marginal osteophytes, endplate sclerosis and facet joint arthropathy — extremely common and often incidental.
🐕Spondylolysis
A defect in the pars interarticularis; on oblique views it looks like a collar on the neck of the "Scottie dog". Often at L5.
➡️Spondylolisthesis
Forward slip of one vertebra on the one below (commonly L5 on S1), graded I–IV by the Meyerding classification (quartiles of slip).
🔀Transitional vertebra
Lumbarisation of S1 or sacralisation of L5 — alters the segment count and can cause labelling errors; note it before any intervention.
🎋Ankylosing spondylitis
Sacroiliitis, marginal syndesmophytes and a fused "bamboo spine". Suspect in young men with inflammatory back pain (night pain, morning stiffness).
💥Vertebral fracture
Loss of vertebral body height / wedging; osteoporotic or traumatic. Consider malignancy if the posterior wall is involved or a pedicle is lost.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph. Lateral lumbosacral view showing grade II anterolisthesis of L5 on S1 with a visible pars defect, and an oblique view demonstrating the broken "Scottie dog" collar.
🚩 Suspected cauda equina syndrome — bilateral sciatica, saddle (perineal) anaesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence, faecal incontinence, and reduced anal tone — is a surgical emergency. It needs urgent MRI and immediate spinal surgery referral. A plain X-ray is useless here and must never delay the MRI. Likewise, back-pain red flags (history of cancer, unexplained weight loss, night pain, fever, IV drug use, progressive neurology) point to malignancy or infection and mandate MRI, not radiographs.
🎓 If a patient with low back pain has no red flags, do not X-ray — reassure, advise on activity and analgesia, and safety-net. If they do have red flags, the answer is almost always MRI, not plain film. The lumbar X-ray earns its gonadal dose only for mechanical structural questions: trauma, spondylolisthesis, deformity, inflammatory screening and hardware assessment.

The single most examinable point about the coccyx X-ray is that you should rarely request one. Coccydynia and suspected coccygeal fracture are treated conservatively whether or not a fracture is seen, so a radiograph delivers a significant pelvic and gonadal radiation dose to answer a question that does not change management. The sacrum, by contrast, is imaged for specific reasons — insufficiency fractures, pelvic ring trauma, sacroiliitis, and tumours — but plain film is insensitive, and MRI or CT is usually the correct investigation.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph: AP sacrum showing the sacral foramina with their smooth curved arcuate lines, the sacroiliac joints, and the coccygeal segments tapering inferiorly.
1Why the coccyx film is usually the wrong request

Coccydynia is largely a clinical diagnosis. A coccygeal fracture is managed identically to a bruise or sprain — analgesia, activity modification, a cushioning "ring" cushion to offload the coccyx when sitting, and reassurance that recovery is slow but usual. Because the result does not alter treatment, the film fails the justification test under IR(ME)R, and the pelvic/gonadal dose is hard to defend.

Isolated coccyx pain after a fall onto the buttocks→Clinical diagnosis + conservative management; no X-ray needed
2Legitimate reasons to image the sacrum

The sacrum earns imaging in defined settings, but the modality matters — plain film misses a great deal.

Sacral insufficiency fracture — elderly/osteoporotic or post-radiotherapy patients. Often occult on plain film; the classic "Honda" or H sign of bilateral sacral ala uptake is seen on bone scan, with MRI/CT far more sensitive.
Pelvic ring / high-energy trauma — the sacrum is a component of the posterior ring; a sacral fracture here may be unstable.
Sacroiliitis — ankylosing spondylitis and other spondyloarthropathies show SI joint erosions, sclerosis and eventual ankylosis.
Tumours — chordoma (the sacrum is its classic site), metastases, and incidental Tarlov (perineural) cysts.
3Reading the sacral film systematically

Work through a small checklist so you do not miss the subtle findings.

◔Arcuate lines
Trace the smooth curved cortical lines above each sacral foramen — disruption or a step suggests a fracture through the ala.
◑SI joints
Assess symmetry, joint space, erosions and sclerosis — the seat of sacroiliitis in spondyloarthropathy.
◕Coccygeal segments
Note alignment and angulation, but remember normal variation is wide and a "fracture" rarely changes care.
●Bone texture
Scan for lytic/sclerotic lesions suggesting metastasis or chordoma; a normal film does not exclude them.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph: coronal STIR MRI of the sacrum showing high-signal bilateral sacral ala oedema in an H/Honda distribution, the appearance of a sacral insufficiency fracture that was invisible on the preceding plain film.
🚩 A sacral fracture as part of a pelvic ring injury after high-energy trauma may be unstable and associated with haemorrhage and neurological injury (cauda equina / sacral plexus) — check perineal sensation and continence and get urgent orthopaedic/pelvic-trauma input. Separately, new sacral pain in an older, osteoporotic or cancer patient should prompt suspicion of an insufficiency fracture or metastasis: image with MRI rather than trusting a normal plain film.
🎓 If your management would be the same whatever the film shows, the film is not justified — coccydynia is the textbook example. Reserve imaging for the sacrum, choose MRI/CT over plain radiography when a fracture or lesion matters, and never let a normal sacral X-ray reassure you in an elderly or oncology patient.
PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY__X-ray Chest:
The PA chest radiograph is the single most requested plain film in medicine and the one you will read most in clinical practice and exams. Get a system, use it every single time, and never let a normal-looking film lull you into skipping a step.

1Technique — why PA and erect
In a postero-anterior (PA) film the X-ray source sits behind the patient and the detector/film is against the chest in front. The patient stands erect at full inspiration with the breath held. Because the heart lies anteriorly, close to the film, it is magnified minimally — so the cardiothoracic ratio measured on a PA film is accurate. An AP film (source in front, film behind, often a sick or portable patient) magnifies the heart and cannot be used to comment on true cardiomegaly.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph.
2Check quality first — RIPE
Before interpreting anything, decide whether the film is adequate. Use RIPE.
Rotation — the spinous processes should sit equidistant between the medial ends of the two clavicles. If not, the patient is rotated and mediastinal contours will be distorted.
Inspiration — count 5–6 anterior ribs or 8–10 posterior ribs above the diaphragm. Fewer means a poor inspiratory effort, crowding the lung markings and mimicking basal shadowing.
Projection — confirm PA rather than AP (look for the marker, scapulae pulled off the lung fields in PA).
Exposure / penetration — the lower thoracic vertebrae should be just faintly visible through the heart. Too white = under-penetrated; too black = over-penetrated.
3Systematic review — ABCDE
Once quality is confirmed, work through the film the same way every time so nothing is missed.
AAirway
Trachea central (slight deviation to the right at the aortic knuckle is normal). Follow it to the carina. Deviation = pushed (effusion, tension pneumothorax) or pulled (collapse, fibrosis).
BBreathing
Compare lung zones (upper/mid/lower) side to side for symmetry. Inspect the pleura for pneumothorax, effusion, consolidation, masses and nodules.
CCardiac
Cardiothoracic ratio should be <50% on a PA film; >50% is cardiomegaly. Trace both heart borders and the mediastinal contour.
DDiaphragm
The right hemidiaphragm is normally higher than the left (liver). Costophrenic angles should be sharp — blunting suggests an effusion. Look for free air under the diaphragm.
EEverything else
Bones (ribs, clavicles, vertebrae), soft tissues, and the review areas — apices, behind the heart, hila, and below the diaphragm.
Loss of a normal border on the film→the silhouette sign — the pathology lies in the lobe adjacent to that border (e.g. a lost right heart border localises to the right middle lobe)
4Hila and common findings
The left hilum is normally higher than the right — if the reverse is true, or a hilum is bulky/dense, suspect a mass or lymphadenopathy. Common patterns to name confidently: consolidation (air bronchograms, silhouette loss), pleural effusion (blunted costophrenic angle with a rising lateral meniscus), pneumothorax (a visible lung edge with absent markings peripherally), a mass, cardiomegaly, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (sarcoid, TB, lymphoma).
📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph.
🚩 Tension pneumothorax is a CLINICAL diagnosis — tracheal deviation away from the affected side, hyperresonance, absent breath sounds and cardiovascular collapse. Decompress immediately; do not wait for a chest X-ray. Likewise, a large effusion or lobar collapse causing respiratory distress needs urgent action, and free air under the diaphragm indicates a perforated viscus requiring urgent surgical review.
🎓 A film is only worth interpreting once you have proven it is technically adequate — always check RIPE before you comment on the lungs, or you will read artefact as disease. And when the clinical picture screams tension pneumothorax, your hands should be reaching for a needle, not the radiology request form.

The AP / portable chest X-ray is the film you meet at the bedside — shot on the sickest patients who cannot get to the radiology department and stand against a PA cassette. Its rules are different, its measurements are unreliable, and its whole reason for existing is often not the lungs at all but the lines and tubes keeping the patient alive. Read every AP film as "different, not just worse."

1Know what "AP / portable" actually means
A standard chest film is PA: patient stands, chest to the cassette, X-ray source ~2 m behind. On a portable film the machine comes to the bed, so the beam enters the front and the film sits behind the patient — antero-posterior. The patient is usually supine or semi-erect in ICU, resus or on the ward, too unwell to stand. Every one of the AP pitfalls below flows from these two facts: the heart is now far from the film, and the patient is lying down.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph: side-by-side AP portable vs PA erect film, showing the enlarged-looking heart, overlying scapulae and "AP SUPINE" label on the portable image.
2The heart is magnified — never diagnose cardiomegaly
Because the heart lies anteriorly and is now further from the film, the beam magnifies it. The cardiothoracic ratio is unreliable on an AP film — a heart that looks big may be entirely normal. This is a classic exam point: you cannot diagnose cardiomegaly on an AP / portable film. If the shadow genuinely looks enlarged, say "apparent cardiomegaly, unreliable on AP projection — correlate with echo or a PA film."
Big-looking heart on a portable film→do NOT call cardiomegaly — magnification artefact until proven otherwise
3Supine changes how fluid and air behave
Gravity still works — but the patient is flat, so free fluid and free air redistribute:
Pleural effusion: instead of a crisp meniscus and blunted costophrenic angle, fluid layers posteriorly across the whole hemithorax — a diffuse "veil" or generalised haziness of that side, with vessels still visible through it. Easy to miss.
Pneumothorax: air rises to the highest point, which when supine is anterior and basal, not the apex. Look for the deep sulcus sign — an abnormally deep, lucent, sharply outlined costophrenic angle on the affected side.
Also expect: scapulae overlying the lung fields, frequent rotation, magnification, and a poorer inspiration than an erect PA — all normal for the projection, none of them pathology.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph: supine film with a right-sided deep sulcus sign (abnormally deep lucent costophrenic angle) and a left-sided hazy "veil" from a layering effusion.
4Its superpower: checking lines and tubes
The portable film exists to answer one question fast at the bedside — is the hardware in the right place? This is where marks are won.
🫁ET tube
Tip ~5 cm above the carina, mid-trachea. Too low = endobronchial (usually right main); too high / in oesophagus = failed airway.
🍽️NG tube
Must bisect the carina, pass below the left hemidiaphragm and tip clearly in the stomach. Never in the bronchi.
💉Central line
Tip at the SVC / right-atrial junction. Always check for a post-insertion pneumothorax.
🩹Drains & devices
Chest drain side-holes inside the pleura; pacemaker / ICD leads and box positioned and intact.
Always label the film AP and state the position (supine / semi-erect) in your read — it tells the next reader why the heart and fluid look the way they do.
🚩 NG tube confirmation before feeding is a patient-safety NEVER EVENT. The tip must sit below the diaphragm / in the stomach — if the tube is in the lungs and feed is given, it is fatal. A mispositioned ET tube (oesophageal or endobronchial) needs immediate correction. And remember: a tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis — decompress on the shocked, deviated-trachea patient; do not wait for the X-ray.
🎓 Read an AP film with the projection in mind: don't measure the heart, hunt the base and the sulcus rather than the apex for fluid and air, and treat every line and tube as the real question. "AP, supine, apparent cardiomegaly unreliable, NG tip below the left hemidiaphragm in the stomach" is the language of a safe bedside read.

The lateral chest radiograph is a supplementary view — never a primary survey film — requested to localise and confirm what the PA has shown or hinted at. Standard technique is a left lateral (left side against the film cassette, minimising cardiac magnification). Its value lies in adding the antero-posterior dimension that the frontal film flattens: it turns a shadow of uncertain depth into a lesion you can assign to a lobe, and it lights up the two big PA "blind spots" behind the heart and behind the sternum.

📷 Image placeholder — normal left lateral chest radiograph, annotated: retrosternal clear space (anterior lucency), retrocardiac space, the two obliquely-running major fissures, right horizontal (minor) fissure, and both hemidiaphragms.
1Localise the lesion to a lobe

A shadow on the PA tells you it is somewhere in that half of the chest, but not how far front or back. On the lateral you use the fissures as boundaries: the oblique (major) fissures run infero-anteriorly on both sides, and on the right the horizontal (minor) fissure separates upper from middle lobe. A lesion sitting anterior to the oblique fissure is in an upper or middle lobe; posterior to it, a lower lobe. Two views also confirm the lesion is real — a true opacity appears on both PA and lateral, whereas a skin fold, nipple or rib artefact does not track across.

Opacity behind the heart on PA is barely visible→the lateral shows it clearly in the retrocardiac space and pins it to a lobe
2The two lucent "clear spaces" that turn white

Two regions are normally dark (lucent) on the lateral because they are mostly air-filled or air-surrounded. Pathology fills them in, so they become whiter. Learn to look for them actively.

Retrosternal clear space — the lucent triangle just behind the sternum. Loss of this lucency (increased whiteness) points to an anterior mediastinal mass — the "terrible Ts": thymoma, teratoma (germ cell), (terrible) lymphoma and retrosternal thyroid.
Spine sign — as your eye travels down the thoracic spine the vertebral bodies should become progressively darker (more lucent). If the lower spine looks whiter/denser than the upper spine, suspect overlying lower lobe pathology (consolidation, collapse or effusion) projected over it.
Diaphragms & hila — the right hemidiaphragm is seen along its whole length; the left hemidiaphragm is obscured anteriorly where the heart sits against it (silhouette effect), so it appears to "disappear" at the front. The hila overlie the mid-thorax.
3Small pleural effusions

Fluid collects in the most dependent recess. The deepest costophrenic recess is the posterior one, seen on the lateral — so a small effusion blunts the posterior costophrenic angle earlier and with less fluid than it takes to blunt the lateral costophrenic angle on the PA. A sharp posterior angle argues against a significant effusion; a meniscus climbing the posterior chest wall confirms one.

PA costophrenic angles look sharp but effusion suspected→check the posterior costophrenic angle on the lateral — it blunts first
📷 Image placeholder — abnormal lateral showing an increased-density lower spine (positive spine sign) with a triangular retrocardiac opacity of left lower lobe collapse, plus posterior costophrenic angle blunting from a small effusion.
🫁Lower lobe collapse
Hidden behind the heart on PA; on the lateral a wedge of increased density with a positive spine sign and posterior displacement of the oblique fissure.
🎯Anterior mediastinal mass
Fills in the retrosternal clear space (whiter). The "terrible Ts" — thymoma, teratoma, lymphoma, thyroid — needing urgent characterisation.
💧Small effusion
Blunted posterior costophrenic angle — detectable with less fluid than on the PA because the posterior recess is deepest.
✅Confirming a lesion
A real nodule/mass appears on two views; artefacts (skin fold, nipple) do not carry over to the lateral.
🚩 A lesion, lobar collapse or a loculated/large effusion confirmed on the lateral warrants onward evaluation, usually CT. An anterior mediastinal mass filling the retrosternal clear space demands urgent work-up — it may be lymphoma or a mass threatening the airway or causing SVC compression.
🎓 The lateral is a problem-solving film, not a screening one: reach for it to answer a specific question the PA raised. Actively interrogate the two lucencies (retrosternal space and the spine sign) and the posterior costophrenic angle — that is where the lateral earns its keep. Remember it is now largely superseded by CT for actually characterising a lesion, so its modern role is to localise, confirm, and decide who needs cross-sectional imaging.

A pneumothorax lets air sit in the pleural space, and a small apical one can hide against fully-inflated lung. The classic trick is the expiratory film: breathe out, the lung shrinks, but the trapped air does not — so the pneumothorax stands out more clearly against a smaller, denser lung. The same principle unmasks an inhaled foreign body causing air-trapping in a child.

📷 Image placeholder — Erect PA CXR showing a right apical pneumothorax: thin white visceral pleural line, absent lung markings peripherally, collapsed lung edge medially.
1Why expiration helps

On inspiration the lung is fully inflated and pleural air is diluted against a large, well-aerated lung — a small pneumothorax is easily missed. On expiration the lung volume falls while the pneumothorax volume stays constant. The pneumothorax therefore becomes relatively larger and more conspicuous against a smaller, denser (whiter) lung.

Small apical rim not seen on inspiratory film→expiratory film makes the rim proportionally bigger and easier to detect

Caveat: modern evidence and BTS guidance suggest routine expiratory films add little over a good inspiratory film. They are used selectively, not as a default extra view.

2CXR signs of pneumothorax

Look for the visceral pleural line — a thin white line running parallel to the chest wall — with absent lung markings peripheral to it (a lucent, black, avascular zone with no vessels running out to the ribs).

Thin white line = the edge of the collapsed lung (visceral pleura).
Black, vessel-free space between that line and the ribs = pleural air.
On a supine film air rises anteriorly → the deep sulcus sign (an abnormally deep, lucent costophrenic angle).
📷 Image placeholder — Supine trauma CXR demonstrating the deep sulcus sign: abnormally deep, lucent left costophrenic angle from anterior pleural air.
3Inhaled foreign body & air trapping

An inhaled foreign body can act as a ball-valve: air enters on inspiration but cannot escape on expiration. This gives unilateral hyperinflation / air trapping that is exaggerated on expiration.

Child, sudden cough/choke, then expiratory CXR→affected lung stays lucent (does NOT deflate) and mediastinum shifts AWAY on expiration

Because the normal lung empties on expiration but the obstructed lung cannot, the contrast between the two is greatest on the expiratory film — the key diagnostic clue in a child with a suspected inhaled foreign body.

4Management of pneumothorax (BTS)

Management depends on symptoms and size and on whether it is primary (no underlying lung disease) or secondary (e.g. COPD). Broad options:

👁️Conservative
Small, minimally symptomatic primary pneumothorax — observe, high-flow oxygen, safety-net and repeat imaging.
💉Needle aspiration
Symptomatic or larger primary pneumothorax — aspirate with cannula in the safe triangle.
🩹Chest drain
Aspiration failed, or a secondary pneumothorax — intercostal drain into the safe triangle.
🚩 Tension pneumothorax — tracheal deviation AWAY from the affected side, hypotension, distended neck veins, hyperresonance and severe respiratory distress. This is a CLINICAL diagnosis and an immediate life threat: perform emergency needle/finger decompression at once. Do NOT wait for or request a chest X-ray.
🎓 On expiration the lung deflates but pleural air does not — so both a small pneumothorax and a ball-valve foreign body become more obvious on the expiratory film. But never let imaging delay treatment of a suspected tension pneumothorax: decompress first, image never.

The instinct with chest-wall trauma is to order a rib X-ray to "see the fracture". Resist it. In UK practice dedicated rib views are usually not indicated for suspected simple rib fractures — confirming an uncomplicated fracture does not change management, and rib fractures are commonly missed on plain film anyway. The real job of imaging is a standard chest X-ray (CXR) to hunt the complications: pneumothorax, haemothorax, contusion and surgical emphysema. Count the injuries only insofar as certain patterns flag high-energy trauma or underlying organ damage.

1Why you don't chase the fracture

An isolated, uncomplicated rib fracture is managed the same way whether or not you can see it on film: adequate analgesia, breathing/incentive-spirometry exercises to prevent basal atelectasis and secondary pneumonia, and conservative healing over ~6 weeks. Dedicated rib views add radiation, cost and delay without altering that plan — and they are insensitive, frequently missing fractures that are present. So the finding does not justify the test.

Well patient, focal chest-wall tenderness, no dyspnoea→Treat clinically; a CXR is to exclude complications, not to "prove" the fracture
2What the CXR is actually for — the complications

Read the standard erect CXR systematically for the things that do change management:

Pneumothorax — visible visceral pleural line with absent lung markings peripherally; look at the apex on an erect film.
Haemothorax — blunting of the costophrenic angle or a rising meniscus/opacification; needs several hundred mL to show on an erect film and much more when supine.
Pulmonary contusion — non-segmental patchy air-space opacification underlying the injured segment, appearing within hours.
Surgical (subcutaneous) emphysema — lucent streaks of gas tracking through the chest-wall soft tissues, often outlining pectoral muscle fibres.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph.
3Flail chest

Flail chest = 3 or more consecutive ribs each fractured in 2 or more places, freeing a segment of chest wall that moves paradoxically (inward on inspiration, outward on expiration). It is fundamentally a clinical diagnosis made by watching the chest wall, not a radiological one, and it is strongly associated with underlying lung contusion and respiratory compromise.

Segment of chest wall sucking inward on inspiration + hypoxia→Flail chest — analgesia, oxygen, escalate for possible ventilatory support
📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph.
4Fracture location tells you what else to worry about

The site of the fracture is more useful than the fact of it. Use location to trigger the right onward assessment.

⬆️1st / 2nd rib or scapula
Protected, well-splinted bones — fracture implies high-energy transfer. Screen for great-vessel/aortic injury and brachial plexus damage.
⬇️Lower ribs 9–12
Overlie solid organs: right → liver; left → spleen; either → kidney. Assess for intra-abdominal injury.
🦴Pathological / lytic
Fracture through a lucent lesion or minimal trauma → suspect metastasis or myeloma.
👶Infant posterior / multiple ages
Posterior rib fractures or multiple fractures of differing ages → strong red flag for non-accidental injury.
🚩 Red flags. Flail chest with respiratory compromise needs urgent analgesia, oxygen and often ITU/ventilatory support. Lower rib fractures mandate assessment for solid-organ injury — consider CT or FAST. Multiple or posterior rib fractures in an infant demand a safeguarding referral, not reassurance.
🎓 The exam-winning line: you do not X-ray to find the rib fracture — you image to find what the fracture did to the lungs, vessels and abdominal organs. A normal-looking rib does not exclude injury, and a visible one rarely changes the plan.

The sternum hides on a frontal chest film — it overlies the spine and mediastinum, so it is almost never assessed properly on a standard PA/AP view. When you actually need to look at it, you ask for a dedicated lateral sternum and an oblique (RAO) view. But the real teaching point is bigger than the bone: a sternal fracture is a flag for significant anterior chest trauma, and the injuries you must not miss lie behind it — the heart, the great vessels, the lungs and the thoracic spine.

📷 Image placeholder — Lateral sternum radiograph showing the manubrium, sternal body and xiphoid in profile against a soft-tissue background; annotate a cortical step in the sternal body and the retrosternal soft-tissue stripe.
1Know why you need a dedicated view

On the frontal chest film the sternum projects directly over the dense vertebral column and mediastinum, so cortical detail is lost. To see it you need to throw it off the spine:

Sternum overlies the spine on PA/AP→request a lateral (best single view of the body/manubrium) plus an oblique / RAO view
Lateral view — profiles the manubrium, sternal body and xiphoid; best for a cortical break or step.
RAO oblique — rotates the sternum clear of the spine and projects it over the homogeneous cardiac shadow.
2Recognise the classic mechanism

A sternal fracture almost always follows blunt anterior chest trauma. The archetype is the steering-wheel / seat-belt injury in a road-traffic collision, where the chest decelerates against the wheel or restraint. It is also seen after CPR.

RTC with chest against steering wheel / seat-belt→high-energy anterior load — actively look for a sternal fracture and its neighbours
3Read the film systematically

Trace the cortex of the manubrium and sternal body; a fracture shows as a break or step in the cortex. Then look behind it.

Cortical break or step in the sternal body or manubrium — the fracture itself.
Retrosternal haematoma — soft-tissue fullness / widened stripe behind the sternum.
Widened mediastinum on the chest film — raises great-vessel injury.
📷 Image placeholder — Sagittal CT of the chest through the midline showing a displaced sternal body fracture with an adjacent retrosternal haematoma, illustrating why CT outperforms plain film.
4Hunt for the associated injuries

The sternum matters mainly as a marker. The concern is what sits behind and around it — and CT chest images the bone and all of these far better than plain film, so in significant trauma CT is preferred.

🫀Blunt cardiac injury
Myocardial contusion — arrhythmia risk. Get an ECG, troponin and cardiac monitoring.
💧Pericardial effusion / tamponade
Instability with an effusion suggests tamponade — an emergency.
🩸Great-vessel injury
Aortic / great-vessel trauma — widened mediastinum; CT angiography.
🫁Pulmonary contusion
Underlying lung bruising — hypoxia; patchy consolidation on CT.
🦴Thoracic spine fracture
Sternum + spine form a ring — a break in one demands a search for a break in the other.
5Consider non-traumatic causes

Not every sternal abnormality is a fracture. In the absence of trauma think:

Metastasis or myeloma — lytic destruction of the sternum.
Infection / osteomyelitis — classically post-sternotomy after cardiac surgery.
SAPHO syndrome — sternocostoclavicular hyperostosis and osteitis.
🚩 A sternal fracture warrants an ECG, troponin and a period of cardiac monitoring to exclude blunt cardiac injury and arrhythmia. Haemodynamic instability with a pericardial effusion suggests tamponade — a surgical emergency. And always image the thoracic spine: the sternum and spine form a ring, so look for a concomitant spinal fracture.
🎓 The sternal fracture is rarely the problem — it is the calling card of significant anterior chest trauma. Treat the fracture as a prompt: ECG, troponin, cardiac monitoring, a low threshold for CT chest, and a deliberate look for a thoracic spine injury.
